Andy Robertson believes Liverpool’s prospects of mounting a serious Premier League title bid under Arne Slot will depend heavily on tightening up defensively. Although the new manager has enjoyed a bright opening with the team keeping clean sheets in both of their first two league matches, the real examination is still ahead, with a demanding visit to Manchester United coming up on Sunday. So far, Ipswich and Brentford have both been kept out, giving Slot an ideal start to life at Anfield, but Robertson knows the level of difficulty is likely to rise sharply at Old Trafford, where Liverpool’s back four could be tested much more seriously. He also pointed out that last season’s campaign showed why defensive improvement matters so much: Liverpool ended up finishing third after conceding 41 goals in 38 games, which was more than the two sides above them, Manchester City and Arsenal. Even so, he feels the early signs under Slot have been encouraging and that the team is already showing a stronger platform.

handle that encouraging start carefully, Robertson said Liverpool must now try to maintain the same standard against stronger opposition and reduce the number of chances they allow. He stressed that keeping another clean sheet, or at least limiting Manchester United’s opportunities, would be an important next step before the season’s rhythm is disrupted by the international break. In his view, the issue last year was not simply the number of goals conceded, but the fact that the side often allowed more openings than Arsenal and Manchester City even while they were still very much in the title conversation. That imbalance, he suggested, eventually made it inevitable that Liverpool would be punished in one or more matches. Robertson’s comments reflect a broader concern that if a team consistently gives opponents too many chances, the defensive record will eventually catch up with them, no matter how strong their attacking play may be.

Looking ahead, the defender’s message is clear: if Liverpool want to remain in the title picture throughout Slot’s first season, they need to turn those promising early performances into a sustained defensive habit. The unbeaten opening, built on two clean sheets, has given supporters a reason to be optimistic, but Robertson is not treating it as proof that the problem has been solved. Instead, he sees it as a foundation that must be strengthened against tougher opponents such as Manchester United and, later, the rest of the league once club football resumes after the break. For Liverpool, the challenge is not just to score and dominate games, but to become more controlled and resilient when under pressure. If they can restrict chances more effectively than they did last year, they may avoid the costly slip that derailed their previous title push and give Slot a genuine opportunity to compete at the very top.
